issues.subcategory: Inconsistent z-value and p-value
issues.description: In Experiment 2, the token-based interaction between specificity and condition is reported as z = 0.60, p < 0.01. A z-value of 0.60 corresponds to a two-tailed p-value of approximately 0.55, not p < 0.01. This is a critical discrepancy that undermines the claim that token-based analyses converge with type-based findings for this interaction.
issues.quote: As predicted, the interaction between specificity and condition was significant, such that the target spelling became used more often in the congruent condition than in the incongruent condition as its specificity increased (B = 1.9, z = 2.8, p < 0.01; for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01)

issues.subcategory: Mismatched values between text and table for go-past time
issues.description: The go-past time congruency effect is reported differently in the text and Table 5. The running text reports B = 41, t = 3.837, while Table 5 reports B = 43, t = 3.76. The raw means in the table imply a difference of 49 ms (507 - 458), which matches neither estimate. At least two of these three values must be wrong.
issues.quote: There was an effect of congruency on go-past time (B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001)

issues.subcategory: Mismatched values between text and table for regressions-out
issues.description: The regressions-out congruency effect is reported as B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < 0.01 in the text, but Table 5 reports B = 0.25, z = 2.65, p < 0.01. These are substantially different estimates and test statistics that could reflect different models or an error in reporting.
issues.quote: The effect of congruency on regressions-out was significant in the expected direction, i.e. incongruent targets were more likely to elicit regressions to earlier regions of the sentence (B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < 0.01).

issues.subcategory: Incorrect formula description for diagnosticity
issues.description: The formula for type diagnosticity is described as dividing the number of words ending in the suffix and falling into a category 'by the total number of words falling into this category.' This formula yields P(suffix | category), not P(category | suffix). However, diagnosticity is defined as the probability of the category given the spelling (cue validity), and the reported values (e.g., -IAN diagnosticity for nouns = 0.54) are consistent with P(category | suffix), not P(suffix | category). Thus, the textual description of the denominator appears to be erroneous, which impedes replicability.
issues.quote: For a particular suffix, type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.

issues.subcategory: Reversed directional predictions for diagnosticity and specificity
issues.description: The authors state that diagnosticity (spelling-to-meaning) should impact spelling production, while specificity (meaning-to-spelling) should impact reading tasks. This is logically reversed: spelling-to-meaning consistency should affect reading (Experiments 1, 3), and meaning-to-spelling consistency should affect spelling (Experiment 2). Indeed, the actual experiments test diagnosticity in reading/categorization and specificity in spelling, contradicting the stated hypothesis. This appears to be a labelling error in the text.
issues.quote: we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the production of spelling, while specificity, a measure of meaning-to-spelling consistency, would impact on tasks involving the mapping of print to meaning (i.e. semantic categorisation, reading).

issues.subcategory: Missing random effects for items
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the mixed model includes only a random intercept for subjects, with no random intercept for items or suffixes. This means that item-level variability is not accounted for, which can inflate Type I error rates. The same issue applies to Experiment 2. Given that the key manipulation is at the suffix level and there are only 10-11 suffixes per condition, failing to account for this clustering is a notable omission.
issues.quote: We included a random intercept for subjects. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial").

issues.subcategory: Uncontrolled pre-target word count difference
issues.description: In Experiment 3, the number of pre-target words differed significantly between congruent and incongruent conditions (4.75 vs 5.23, p < 0.05). Since the critical eye-movement measures (go-past time, regressions-out) reflect integration of the target word with preceding context, more pre-target context in the incongruent condition could provide stronger category expectations, confounding the congruency effect. This was acknowledged but not controlled for in the analyses.
issues.quote: Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05).

issues.subcategory: Proportion reported as percentage
issues.description: Average comprehension accuracy is reported as 0.86% with a range from 0.66% to 0.98%. These are clearly proportions (86%), not percentages. Reporting 0.86% suggests accuracy below 1%, which would indicate participants were not reading the sentences.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%).

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent entropy regression test
issues.description: The authors report the slope of the entropy regression as 0.9 (SE = 0.04) and test whether it differs from 1. Using the reported values, t = (0.9 - 1)/0.04 = -2.5, and F = t² = 6.25. However, they report F(1) = 7.44. This discrepancy suggests either the SE or the F-value is incorrectly reported.
issues.quote: We found that the regression line has a slope of 0.9 (SE = 0.04, t = 25.32, p < 0.0001), and that this slope is significantly different from 1 (F (1) = 7.44, p < 0.01).

issues.subcategory: No pre-registration or correction for multiple comparisons
issues.description: In Experiment 3, six eye-movement measures are tested without correction for multiple comparisons. The authors acknowledge they did not have concrete predictions about which measures would be affected. No pre-registration is mentioned for any of the three experiments. Given the number of measures in Experiment 3 and the exploratory nature of the analysis, there is considerable analytic flexibility that inflates the risk of false positives.
issues.quote: We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected by the diagnosticity manipulation, so we chose to monitor a variety of typically studied measures

issues.subcategory: Learning claim unsupported by cross-sectional design
issues.description: The authors claim that readers 'learn and subsequently rely on morphological cues' and that knowledge was 'acquired through implicit statistical learning processes.' However, the experiments are cross-sectional demonstrations that adults possess this knowledge, not that they acquired it through statistical learning. A training or developmental study would be needed to support claims about learning mechanisms.
issues.quote: We have shown that the average reader learns and subsequently relies on morphological cues to class even without explicit instruction to do so (see our spelling and eye tracking data) suggesting that these cues facilitate access to meaning.

issues.subcategory: High missing data rate without analysis
issues.description: In Experiment 1, 11.7% of data points were missing due to timeouts or non-response button presses. This is a high rate for a simple binary classification task with a 2-second timeout. There is no analysis of whether missingness was related to condition (noun vs. adjective suffixes) or diagnosticity, which could bias the results.
issues.quote: 11.7% of data points were missing due to timeouts or button presses that did not correspond to a response

issues.subcategory: Lexical category equated with meaning
issues.description: The title and framing discuss 'meaningful regularities' and the relationship between 'spelling and meaning,' but the operationalization is limited to lexical category (noun, adjective, verb). Lexical category is one syntactic/semantic property of words, but the broader claims about spelling-meaning relationships are not warranted by evidence limited to category information. The discussion acknowledges this somewhat, but the title and abstract overclaim.
issues.quote: This paper focuses on one aspect of word meaning, specifically, lexical category (e.g., noun, adjective, verb; see Baayen et al., 2011, for a similar conceptualisation of "meaning").

issues.subcategory: Diagnosticity correlation computation unclear
issues.description: The correlation between diagnosticity and specificity is reported as 0.53 (p < 0.0001), but it is not clear how these values were computed. Each suffix has diagnosticity values for three categories (noun, adjective, verb) and specificity values for three categories. The authors do not specify whether they used the maximum value, the value for the dominant category, or all values. This is important for interpreting and replicating the analysis.
issues.quote: The correlation between the type variables is 0.53, p < 0.0001; that between the token variables – 0.47, p < 0.0001.

issues.subcategory: No counterbalancing of items across conditions in Experiment 2
issues.description: In Experiment 2, each participant saw all 66 sentences, with particular nonwords always assigned to the same condition (congruent or incongruent). There was no counterbalancing of items across conditions (e.g., via a Latin square), meaning that item-specific properties other than the suffix are fully confounded with condition. While the phonological sequence was the same across conditions, other aspects of the sentence frames differ systematically.
issues.quote: Each subject saw all 66 sentences.

issues.subcategory: Overclaiming functional advantage of English spelling
issues.description: The authors claim that the proliferation of spellings in English 'may actually be functional' for conveying meaningful information. However, the entropy analysis shows only a very small difference (mean H_spelling = 0.61 vs mean H_sound = 0.63), and the slope of 0.9 is only marginally different from 1. This modest difference is used to support the strong theoretical claim that spelling-sound inconsistency 'maximises the transmission of meaningful information,' which seems disproportionate to the evidence.
issues.quote: the spellings of derivational suffixes generally yield better prediction of lexical category (mean H=0.61) than do their spoken realisations (mean H=0.63).

issues.subcategory: Small number of suffixes per condition limits generalizability
issues.description: Experiment 1 uses 10 noun-diagnostic and 10 adjective-diagnostic suffixes; Experiment 2 uses 11 suffixes; Experiment 3 uses 10 noun and 10 adjective suffixes. With so few suffixes per condition, the graded diagnosticity/specificity analyses are based on very limited ranges of items, reducing statistical power for detecting graded effects and limiting generalizability to the broader set of 154 suffixes.
issues.quote: Twenty suffixes diagnostic for the noun or adjective category were selected

issues.subcategory: Incomplete reporting of separate category analyses
issues.description: In Experiment 2, the authors report a significant interaction between specificity and condition, and state there was no effect of specificity in the incongruent condition. However, the effect of specificity in the congruent condition is not reported separately with full statistics, making it difficult to evaluate the pattern fully.
issues.quote: there was no effect of specificity in the incongruent condition.

issues.subcategory: Verb filler claim inconsistent with suffix properties
issues.description: The authors justify not analyzing verb filler items in Experiment 3 by stating that 'the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category (i.e. diagnosticity is less than 0.5).' However, the verb suffix –ate has a diagnosticity of 0.687 for verbs (Appendix A), and several other verb fillers may also exceed 0.5. This justification is inaccurate for at least some of the filler suffixes used.
issues.quote: the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category (i.e. diagnosticity is less than 0.5)

issues.subcategory: No random slopes in mixed models
issues.description: Across all three experiments, only random intercepts are included in the mixed models (for subjects, and for suffixes in Experiment 3). No random slopes for the effect of condition by subjects or items are included. Barr et al. (2013) have shown that omitting random slopes can inflate Type I error rates substantially, especially when the design supports their inclusion.
issues.quote: All models included trial order as a main effect, and random intercepts for subjects and for suffixes.

issues.subcategory: Sample limited to university students
issues.description: All three experiments used undergraduate students from a single university. The claims about 'skilled readers' sensitivity' and 'the average reader' are broader than what this convenience sample supports. Reading experience, education level, and vocabulary size vary considerably in the general population and could modulate sensitivity to these regularities.
issues.quote: We have shown that the average reader learns and subsequently relies on morphological cues to class even without explicit instruction to do so

issues.subcategory: Effect sizes not reported
issues.description: No effect sizes (e.g., odds ratios, Cohen's d, R²) are reported for any of the three experiments. Reporting only regression coefficients and z/t values makes it difficult to assess the practical significance of the observed effects.
issues.quote: Results showed a main effect of suffix condition such that noun-diagnostic suffixes elicited more "noun" responses (B = -1.57, z = -4.224, p < 0.0001)

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 may confound morphological and non-morphological cues
issues.description: The authors acknowledge they did not include non-pseudoaffixed controls in Experiment 1, meaning it is unclear whether participants' categorization is driven by suffix-level morphological knowledge or by lower-level orthographic pattern statistics. The authors note this limitation but still interpret results in morphological terms.
issues.quote: We did not include non-pseudoaffixed words because the goal of this experiment was not to adjudicate between types of cues used in lexical category judgement (e.g. orthographic vs morphological).

issues.subcategory: Experiment 3 marginal effect interpreted as supporting hypothesis
issues.description: In Experiment 3, the diagnosticity effect on go-past time in the incongruent condition is described as a 'trend' (p = 0.13). This marginal result is presented as evidence supporting the hypothesis that diagnosticity modulates the congruency effect, but a p-value of 0.13 does not provide convincing evidence for this simple effect.
issues.quote: whereas there was a trend towards an effect in the incongruent condition (B = 36.35, t = 1.58, p = 0.13).
